title: GLP-1 weight loss pills arrive in Australia: what you should know
transcript:
Host:
This is The Guardian.
Speaker 1:
I'm not Haidar coming to you from Gadigal land, and this is the Full Story.
Injectable weight-loss medications like Ozempic or Wegovy have transformed chronic weight management and are a staple on the red carpet.
In Australia, the only way to receive these drugs, known as GLP-1s, has been a weekly jab.
But now, the needle is no longer the only option.
With the Therapeutic Goods Administration approving not one, but two oral GLP-1 weight-loss pills.
Well, a Western Sydney chemist is among the first in Australia to stock the Wegovy weight-loss pill.
Wegovy weight loss pill will be rolled out in pharmacies today, hitting shelves sooner than expected.
It comes just days after a similar In a country where roughly two in three adults are living with overweight or obesity, the arrival of a daily tablet removes one of the biggest barriers to treatment: the fear and inconvenience of injecting.
But what's the fine print on these medications?
And what impact will they have across health, the economy, and cultural attitudes towards weight loss?
Today, Medical Editor Melissa Davey on how these new pills actually work, who they're meant for, and what their arrival means for Australia's health landscape.
It's Monday, November 23.
Host:
Mel, it's great to have you on Full Story.
Melissa Davey:
Thanks for having me back.
Host:
So, just this month, two new weight-loss drugs were approved for use in Australia.
One is already available in some pharmacies.
These GLP-1 medications are pills that are taken in oral form.
Is that a positive development from your perspective?
Melissa Davey:
There are doctors saying this is positive for people who want a needle-free option, and that having a wider variety of weight loss drugs available is a good thing.
Of course, the ones that have been available have been an injection form.
Pills are generally cheaper to produce, so there's a hope I think that lower production costs and more competition will eventually, down the track, bring prices down, and that will make the medications more accessible overall.
But because these weight loss pills are not covered by Australia's Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme, so that's where the cost is partly subsidized by the government, these will initially be very expensive medications up there in price with um with the injections, costing sometimes hundreds of dollars a month.
So the pills come with some of the the similar questions and concerns as injections do around affordability and side effects and long-term impacts and sustainability.
So overall doctors are saying it's a positive development, but there are all those things to keep in mind.
Host:
Okay, let's talk about some of those things.
Foundeo got the tick of approval from the TGA last week.
Wegovy was approved earlier in the month.
How do these pills actually work?
What are they doing inside the body to encourage weight loss?
Melissa Davey:
Yes, so Wegovy pill, that has the same active ingredient as the weight loss GLP-1 injections and that's a peptide called semaglutide.
And then there's also another similar pill available from a different brand, but that one's only approved for diabetes.
So this Wegovy pill is the first kind of oral semaglutide pill specifically approved for weight loss.
Semaglutide is a peptide and peptides are chemical messengers, I guess, in the body.
Semaglutide activates GLP-1 receptors.
And these receptors in the body, among other things, reduce appetite, they slow stomach emptying and this contributes to weight loss.
One of the difficulties in making a semaglutide pill is that the stomach breaks down the peptide really quickly, it doesn't survive digestion.
Getting it into the bloodstream has been difficult, so it's quite a high-dose pill and it's also got this protective absorption enhanced built into it, so the medication can actually work.
But stopping the semaglutide from being destroyed was a barrier initially to creating these medications in pill form.
So the other pill, Foundeo, that also targets GLP-1 receptors, but it doesn't use peptides to do it.
So it's less fragile, it can survive digestion, and once it's absorbed by the body it acts in a very similar way.
It suppresses appetite, it slows digestion, it's working on the same receptors.
They both are very similar in terms of side effects, you know, bloating, digestive issues, potential issues with nutrient absorption, muscle loss, so they've got similar effects in terms of the weight loss and similar effects in terms of side effects as well.
Host:
So, Mel, who have they been approved for?
Because it's not the case that anyone can get their hands on these new pills.
Melissa Davey:
Yes.
Both the Foundeo and Wegovy pill have been approved for weight management, provided people meet certain criteria including body mass index thresholds.
Foundeo is approved for those with type 2 diabetes.
Wegovy has been approved for reducing cardiovascular disease risk as well.
So they are they're both for weight loss, but they have some additional conditions that they might be prescribed for.
Host:
Aside from the way that they're taken, are there other differences between these pills and the GLP-1s that are already on the market as injections?
Melissa Davey:
In terms of the difference between the pills and the GLP-1 injections, so they all target the same GLP-1 receptors as we discussed.
All similar side effect profiles and concerns, and similar impact on weight loss.
They're all prescribed for weight management for those who meet certain criteria.
There are differences between the pills in terms of when they can be taken.
So doctors will give specific advice to patients that should be followed, but but generally, Foundeo can be taken anytime of the day, with or without food.
Its active ingredient isn't as sensitive to being destroyed during digestion, um as the Wegovy pill.
For those reasons we discussed, the Wegovy pill has to be taken in the morning on an empty stomach before other medications.
There's a little bit of, um a little bit of complexity around when to take it.
Some of the medications have additional conditions they can be prescribed for other than weight loss.
There are those differences between them.
Some of the semaglutide injections, they're also approved for cardiovascular disease risk, whereas some of the other GLP-1s are not.
So there are those differences, but broadly they are very similar in terms of how they work, their side effects, and their overall impact on weight loss.
Host:
Mel, we know that people have found ways to circumvent, you know, getting a prescription to get their hands on some of these GLP-1s.
For many, there would be a temptation to use these weight loss drugs because shedding kilos through diet and exercise alone can be hard.
It can be slow.
It requires long-term discipline and dedication.
But should people be using them if they don't have chronic weight management, diabetes, or obesity?
Melissa Davey:
No one should be using them outside of prescription from their doctor, of course.
Um, but medical guidelines in Australia and globally advise against using GLP-1 medications outside of the conditions that we've been talking about.
And it's because of a number of reasons including side effects.
So if you have a long-term chronic health condition such as overweight and obesity and that carries a real risk of disability and related health issues that people might already be experiencing, those side effects might be something that a doctor and a patient decide are worth managing because of all of the benefits of taking the medication.
For people who don't need them, it's exposing them to risks of quite sometimes severe and unpleasant side effects, all those gastrointestinal issues we've flagged, things like vomiting, bloating, diarrhea, those kinds of things.
But it also these these medications also have an impact on muscle mass and bone density.
We need muscle mass and strong bones to protect us from injury and they're also really important for our metabolism.
So if you start to disrupt those systems of the body by taking these medications, you're actually contradicting yourself.
You're disrupting all the functions of the body that really work to protect you, to keep your metabolism running, to keep you healthy and keep you fit and well.
Muscle is really important for metabolism, it's important for blood sugar control.
And so being on these drugs can have a really significant impact on on muscle mass.
You know, that's why you'll see recommendations for people who are legitimately just prescribed the drugs to do some form of weight training, if their doctor advises it.
The bone and muscle systems, they're quite closely related, they impact on each other and so when you lose muscle, that can have a real impact on your bone health.
And then once your bones become impacted, it increases your risk of injury, things like um fractures, osteoporosis.
There is a real risk of disrupting these really important systems that keep you healthy, keep you strong, keep you fit, and also really are important as you age to keep you well as well.
If you're taking these drugs and you don't need them, you're disrupting that.

Can you talk to me about that?
Why not?
